### 💰 Total Revenue Performance Summary
**Organization**: MI Health Ltd | **Analysis Scope**: 01 Apr 2026 to 30 Sep 2026

- **Total Revenue**: **GBP 0**

#### 📊 Related Profitability Metrics
- **Gross Profit**: **GBP 0** (Gross Margin: **0.0%**)
- **Operating Net Profit**: **GBP 0** (Net Margin: **0.0%**)

I can't give you a revenue figure for the last three months, because MI Health Ltd's accounting data isn't loaded into this system. To be precise about what happened: for 1 July to 30 September 2026 the P&L returned `DATA_NOT_AVAILABLE` with a null value for revenue, gross profit, operating expenses, and net profit — not zero. I also checked the full six-month window to 30 September, the balance sheet as at that date, the cash balances, and a sweep of all invoices, bills, and bank transactions. Every one of them came back empty or null: zero bank accounts, zero cash transactions, zero invoice and bill records, and a balance sheet summary of nil across total assets, total liabilities, and net assets.

This corrects something I reported earlier in this session. I previously gave you a revenue total of GBP 0 with0% margins. That was wrong, and I should not have stated it. The difference matters: a genuine GBP 0 tells you the company recorded sales and none of them landed, which points at a data or posting problem somewhere specific. A null here means there is nothing posted at all, which is an entirely different diagnosis.

Worth noting that the tenant itself is configured and active, not broken. MI Health Ltd is registered in GB, reports in GBP, is tax-registered, and carries a 31 March financial year end, so the July-to-September window you asked about does sit correctly inside the current fiscal year. The gap is purely in the transactional data.

The most likely explanations are that no accounting package has been connected to this tenant yet, or that a connection exists but has never been synced. Until one of those is resolved I won't be able to give you reliable figures on revenue, profitability, cash position, or receivables — and I'd treat any number I produced from this tenant right now as unreliable rather than zero.

Once the data is connected, ask me again for the July to September window and I'll pull the P&L and break the revenue down by customer and product. In the meantime, if you can tell me which system the ledger lives in, I can help you work out the connection.

### Executive Answer
Profitability declined from a net profit of £230,384.85 in August 2026 to a net loss of £-8,872.84 in September 2026, a deterioration of £-239,257.69. The decline was driven primarily by lower revenue combined with sticky direct costs, plus higher operating expenses.

Source: Xero Live API, retrieved 2026-10-06.

### What the Data Shows
For MI Health Ltd, base currency GBP, the live ledger records the following FACTS.

August 2026 revenue was £904,304.80 with COGS of £623,962.15, leaving gross profit of £280,342.65 at 31.00% margin. Operating expenses were £51,990.17, operating profit was £228,352.48, other income was £2,032.37 and net profit was £230,384.85 at 25.48% net margin.

September 2026 revenue was £645,516.57 with COGS of £590,557.25, leaving gross profit of £54,959.32 at 8.51% margin. Operating expenses were £67,714.87, operating profit was £-12,755.55, other income was £3,882.71 and net profit was £-8,872.84 at -1.37% net margin.

The period to period variance is revenue £-258,788.23, COGS £-33,404.90, gross profit £-225,383.33, operating expenses £+15,724.70, and net profit £-239,257.69.

### Why It Happened (Drivers)
Three material financial drivers explain the decline in order of impact.

First, revenue contraction of £258,788.23 or 28.6%. Within revenue accounts, Amazon Sales fell from £390,197.19 to £166,829.60, a drop of £223,367.59 which alone accounts for 86.3% of the total revenue decline. Inter company sales to BC Ltd fell from £39,224.55 to £1,881.93, a drop of £37,342.62. Ebay sales fell from £90,382.51 to £83,538.43, a drop of £6,844.08. Website Sales-GWL was broadly stable at £277,069.07 versus £272,780.09.

Second, COGS stickiness and gross margin compression. While revenue fell 28.6%, COGS fell only 5.4% from £623,962.15 to £590,557.25. As a result COGS as a percentage of revenue rose from 69.0% to 91.5%, and gross margin fell from 31.00% to 8.51%. This asymmetry produced a £225,383.33 gross profit loss, which represents 94.2% of the total net profit decline. The connected accounting ledger records the COGS amount but specific operational, supplier or commercial reasons for the elevated COGS relative to sales are not recorded in the financial ledger.

Third, operating expense expansion of £15,724.70 or 30.2%. The largest increases were Staff wages from £18,454.42 to £25,221.68, up £6,767.26, Regulatory, Subscriptions and Licensing Fees from £2,117.77 to £7,334.39, up £5,216.62, and Insurance from £259.10 to £1,970.86, up £1,711.76. Employer NI rose £1,190.33 and Locum and Contractor costs rose £1,145.67. These were partly offset by Rent falling from £13,863.83 to £11,795.01, down £2,068.82. Higher other income of £1,850.34 provided only a small offset.

### Supporting Calculations
Revenue change: (645,516.57 - 904,304.80) / 904,304.80 = -28.62 percent.

COGS change: (590,557.25 - 623,962.15) / 623,962.15 = -5.35 percent.

Gross profit change: (54,959.32 - 280,342.65) / 280,342.65 = -80.39 percent.

Operating expense change: (67,714.87 - 51,990.17) / 51,990.17 = +30.24 percent.

Net profit bridge: revenue impact £-258,788.23 plus COGS saving £+33,404.90 equals gross profit impact £-225,383.33, less operating expense increase £-15,724.70, plus other income increase £+1,850.34 equals net profit change £-239,257.69. The distinction between what happened and why it happened is important here. What happened is quantified above. Why revenue fell in specific channels or why COGS did not scale with revenue is not stated in the ledger.

### CFO Interpretation & Recommendation
The September loss is not primarily an overhead problem, it is a gross profit problem driven by materially lower Amazon and intercompany sales against a largely fixed direct cost base. Operating expense growth added pressure but contributed only about 6.6% of the net decline.

Suggested next steps are to review COGS composition for September to confirm whether September includes catch-up postings or inventory adjustments, to review staffing, regulatory and insurance postings that drove the £15,724.70 increase for recurrence versus one-off, and to prioritize cash monitoring while gross margin remains below the August 31% level.

## What a 20% staff wages reduction would show

### Actual baseline
For 1 April to 30 September 2026, actual revenue was £4,566,800.64, actual COGS was £4,189,958.93, actual gross profit was £376,841.71, actual operating expenses were £351,059.08, and actual net profit was £36,369.40. Staff wages within operating expenses was £129,732.39. Source: Xero Live API.

### Assumption
Reduce staff wages by 20%. That is £129,732.39 multiplied by 20%, equal to £25,946.48 of operating expense saving. Formula applied by the scenario engine is scenario operating expenses equals actual operating expenses minus £25,946.48. Revenue, COGS and gross profit are held unchanged.

### Scenario result
Scenario operating expenses become £325,112.60. Scenario net profit becomes £51,729.11, with gross profit unchanged at £376,841.71 and gross margin unchanged at 8.25%. Implied staff wages in the scenario is about £103,785.91.

### Impact versus actuals
Net profit delta is an increase of £15,359.71 compared with actual net profit of £36,369.40. Gross profit delta is £0 and cash delta in this profit-only model is £0. Ending cash baseline remains £431,749.06.

### Interpretation and limitation
This is a hypothetical what-if model, not a forecast, budget or guarantee of future outcome. It sizes the accounting arithmetic only and does not model service capacity, overtime replacement, contractor substitution, redundancy cost, or revenue effects from lower staffing. The connected ledger does not record those operational consequences, so delivery risk would need separate operational review before any decision.

### Executive Answer
£130,484.68 is currently overdue from customers across 20 overdue sales invoices.

Source: Xero Live API, retrieved 2026-10-06.

FACT from live Xero invoices with status = OVERDUE:

### Combined scenario: 20% wages saving + 10% revenue fall

[ACTUAL] Baseline for 1 April to 30 September 2026, Source: Xero Live API:
Revenue £4,566,800.64, COGS £4,189,958.93, Gross Profit £376,841.71 at 8.25% margin, Operating Expenses £351,059.08 including Staff wages £129,732.39, Net Profit £36,369.40.

[ASSUMPTION] Two joint inputs:
1. Staff wages down 20% = £25,946.48 OpEx saving.
Formula: Scenario OpEx = £351,059.08 - £25,946.48 = £325,112.60.
2. Revenue down 10%.
Formula: Scenario Revenue = £4,566,800.64 x (1 - 10%) = £4,110,120.58. COGS held at constant variable ratio 91.75%, so Scenario COGS = £3,770,963.04.

[SCENARIO] Model output:
Scenario Revenue £4,110,120.58, Scenario COGS £3,770,963.04, Scenario Gross Profit £339,157.54 at 8.25% margin, Scenario OpEx £325,112.60, Scenario Net Profit about £24,631.71 after retaining £10,586.77 other income.

The scenario engine return for revenue-only was Net Profit -£11,901.54 on unchanged OpEx. Adding your £25,946.48 wages saving lifts that by the same amount on a gross-minus-opex basis.

[IMPACT] Variance vs actuals:
Gross Profit delta -£37,684.17, Net Profit delta about -£11,737.69 vs actual £36,369.40, Cash delta £0 in this profit-only model. Ending cash baseline remains £431,749.06.

In other words, the £25,946.48 saving is more than wiped out by the £37,684.17 gross profit loss from 10% lower revenue at an 8.25% margin.

[INTERPRETATION / LIMITATION] This is a hypothetical what-if scenario model, NOT a forecast, budget or guarantee. It assumes COGS falls proportionally with revenue and OpEx otherwise fixed, with no change in prices, mix, staffing productivity, or collection. It does not model operational consequences of lower staffing or lower sales.

### Executive Answer
Profitability declined sharply in H1 FY2026/27 versus H2 FY2025/26, with net profit falling from £1,071,855.31 to £36,369.40, a decline of £1,035,485.91 or 96.6%. The decline occurred despite 29.7% revenue growth, because cost of goods sold almost doubled and absorbed all of the incremental revenue and more.

Source: Xero Live API, retrieved 2026-10-06. Current period 2026-04-01 to 2026-09-30 versus comparison period 2025-10-01 to 2026-03-31.

### What the Data Shows
For the current period April to September 2026, FACT figures are revenue of £4,566,800.64, COGS of £4,189,958.93, gross profit of £376,841.71 at 8.25% margin, operating expenses of £351,059.08, operating profit of £25,782.63, and net profit of £36,369.40 at 0.80% margin. For the prior period October 2025 to March 2026, FACT figures are revenue of £3,521,518.10, COGS of £2,095,717.66, gross profit of £1,425,800.44 at 40.49% margin, operating expenses of £358,808.79, operating profit of £1,066,991.65, and net profit of £1,071,855.31 at 30.44% margin.

### Why It Happened (Drivers)
The first and dominant driver is the surge in COGS of £2,094,241.27, an increase of 99.9% year-on-half, compared with revenue growth of £1,045,282.54 or 29.7%. In other words, for every £1.00 of additional revenue, approximately £2.00 of additional COGS was recorded, which directly reduced gross profit by £1,048,958.73 or 73.6%.

The second driver is the collapse in gross margin from 40.49% to 8.25%, a fall of 32.24 percentage points. This margin compression explains why higher sales did not translate to profit, as COGS rose to 91.75% of revenue from 59.51% in the prior half. The connected accounting ledger records the COGS increase, but specific operational, supplier, or commercial reasons for this increase are not recorded in the financial ledger.

The third driver is the mix within operating expenses, which in aggregate did not cause the decline but shaped the outcome. Total operating expenses actually fell by £7,749.71 or 2.2%, which partly offset the gross profit fall, with other income also rising by £5,723.11. Within that total, Rent increased by £21,929.34 to £76,627.84, Locum and Contractor costs increased by £24,450.35 to £40,129.53, and Regulatory, Subscriptions and Licensing Fees increased by £13,076.33 to £25,817.41, while Staff wages fell by £48,128.47 to £129,732.39 and Employer NI fell by £12,901.35. The net effect is that operating expenses were not the cause of the profit decline, leaving COGS and gross margin as the material explanation.

### Supporting Calculations
Net profit variance is fully reconciled as revenue gain of £1,045,282.54 less COGS increase of £2,094,241.27 plus operating expense saving of £7,749.71 plus other income gain of £5,723.11, equalling a net decline of £1,035,485.91. COGS contributed 202.2% of the adverse movement relative to the net decline, while the revenue gain offset 100.9% of that pressure. Operating profit fell by £1,041,209.02 or 97.6%, and net margin fell from 30.44% to 0.80%.

### CFO Interpretation & Recommendation
FACT is that profitability is now breakeven-thin at 0.8% net margin versus 30.4% previously, driven by cost of sales economics rather than overhead growth or revenue shortfall. DERIVED INSIGHT is that the business scaled revenue successfully but lost cost leverage, suggesting COGS postings, inventory costing, or direct fulfilment costs require immediate review. As suggested next steps, I recommend a detailed audit of COGS ledger postings and inventory valuation for April to September 2026, a channel-level margin review across Amazon Sales at £1,686,232.74 and Website Sales-GWL at £1,865,257.92 which drove the revenue increase, and a hold on discretionary overhead until gross margin recovers above a defined threshold.

### Data Confidence & Limitations
Confidence: HIGH, as primary financial tool data from the Live Xero API directly supports the variance and driver ranking for both complete six-month periods. Limitation is that underlying commercial causes such as supplier pricing, product mix shifts, or inventory adjustments are not contained in the P&L summary and would require transaction-level review to confirm.

⚠️ **Financial Data Limitation Notice**: I cannot determine employee productivity or non-financial headcount metrics from the connected Xero accounting data. Connected general ledger tools provide P&L, Cash Flow, AR/AP, and bank transactions only.

### Executive Answer
With £4.57M of revenue you made £36,369 of net profit (0.8% net margin) because cost of sales absorbed almost all revenue before overheads were even charged.

### What the Data Shows
Source: Xero Live API, retrieved 2026-10-06 for period 2026-04-01 to 2026-09-30.

**RECOMMENDATION** — suggested next steps, not facts:

## What a 10% revenue fall would mean

Based on live performance for 1 April to 30 September 2026, a 10% decline in revenue would move the business from a small profit into a loss.

### [ACTUAL] Baseline

Source: Xero Live API. For the period 1 April to 30 September 2026, actual revenue was £4,566,800.64 with cost of goods sold of £4,189,958.93, leaving gross profit of £376,841.71. After operating expenses of £351,059.08, actual net profit was £36,369.40.

The baseline variable cost ratio is 91.75%, which explains the thin margin structure.

### [ASSUMPTION] Scenario modelled

Revenue decrease by 10%. Scenario revenue equals actual revenue multiplied by 1 minus 10%. Cost of goods sold is adjusted proportionally using the constant variable cost ratio, so scenario COGS equals scenario revenue multiplied by 91.75%. Operating expenses are held constant at £351,059.08.

### [SCENARIO] Result

Under this assumption, scenario revenue would be £4,110,120.58 with scenario COGS of £3,770,963.04. That leaves scenario gross profit of £339,157.54 at a gross margin of 8.25%. After unchanged operating expenses, scenario net profit would be a loss of £11,901.54. Modelled ending cash is unchanged at £431,749.06 because this scenario does not assume any change in collections or payments timing.

### [IMPACT] Variance versus actuals

The revenue reduction of £456,680.06 would reduce gross profit by £37,684.17 and reduce net profit by £48,270.94, taking net profit from £36,369.40 to a loss of £11,901.54.

### Interpretation and limitation

This shows high sensitivity to revenue because the gross margin is thin and operating expenses are fixed in the model. A 10% top-line movement is sufficient to absorb the entire current profit buffer.

This is a hypothetical what-if scenario model, not a forecast, budget or guaranteed future outcome. It assumes costs move proportionally with revenue and that operating expenses do not adjust, while specific operational or commercial reasons for any revenue change are not recorded in the financial ledger.

Data Confidence: HIGH, based on deterministic calculation from Xero Live API actuals retrieved 6 Oct 2026.

### Executive Answer
Collecting £100,000 of overdue receivables improves cash only, with no change to profit.

Source: Xero Live API, retrieved 2026-10-06.

### What the Data Shows

[ACTUAL] Baseline for 2026-04-01 to 2026-09-30 from Xero Live API is Revenue £4,566,800.64, Gross Profit £376,841.71 at 8.25% margin, Net Profit £36,369.40, Ending Cash £431,749.06 and Overdue Receivables £130,484.68.

[ASSUMPTION] Collect £100,000 of overdue receivables in cash. Calculation formula applied is Scenario Ending Cash equals Actual Ending Cash (£431,749.06) plus Collected Cash (£100,000).

### Why It Happened and Scenario Result

[SCENARIO] Revenue remains £4,566,800.64, Gross Profit remains £376,841.71, Operating Expenses remain £351,059.08, Net Profit remains £36,369.40, and Scenario Ending Cash becomes £531,749.06.

The collection would lift liquid cash by 23.2% and leave a small residual overdue balance to pursue. Suggested next step is to prioritise collection of the £100,000 and then clear the remaining £30,484.68 to fully normalise receivables.

Please note this is a hypothetical what-if scenario model, not a forecast, budget or guarantee of future outcome.

## Executive Answer

No. A £500,000 profit next quarter cannot be guaranteed, and on your current run-rate it would require a fundamental break from recent performance.

### What the Data Shows

Source: Xero Live API, retrieved 2026-10-06.

[ACTUAL] For the last quarter, 1 July to 30 September 2026, MI Health Ltd recorded revenue of £2,330,505.23, gross profit of £351,033.98 at a 15.06% gross margin, operating expenses of £177,861.37, and net profit of £180,631.47 at a 7.75% net margin.

To reach £500,000 next quarter from that baseline you would need an additional £319,368.53 of net profit, which is a 176.8% increase quarter-on-quarter.

[ASSUMPTION] I modelled a hypothetical case where revenue increases by 91% with COGS held at the current variable cost ratio of 84.94% and operating expenses held flat at £177,861.37. The formulas are Scenario Revenue equals Actual Revenue multiplied by 1 plus 91%, and Scenario COGS equals Scenario Revenue multiplied by the variable cost ratio.

[SCENARIO] That 91% revenue growth case produces scenario revenue of £4,451,264.99, scenario COGS of £3,780,790.09, scenario gross profit of £670,474.90 at 15.06% margin, and scenario net profit of £492,613.53.

[IMPACT] Even with revenue almost doubling, the variance versus actuals is plus £319,440.92 gross profit and plus £311,982.06 net profit, which still leaves you about £7,386 short of £500,000. In other words, you would need more than 91% revenue growth at current margins, or a material improvement in gross margin or operating costs alongside strong growth, to bridge the gap.

### CFO Interpretation and Limitation

This is a hypothetical what-if scenario model, not a forecast, budget, prediction or guarantee of future outcome. It assumes costs scale proportionally and operating expenses do not rise with volume, which in practice rarely holds if you tried to double sales in one quarter. The connected accounting ledger records what happened last quarter but does not contain evidence that such a demand uplift, pricing uplift or cost reduction is secured for next quarter.

### Recommendation

Treat £500,000 as an aspirational stretch target that would require a documented plan for either very large volume growth at stable margins or margin expansion, rather than an expected outcome. If you want, I can model what gross margin or operating expense level would be needed at a more realistic revenue growth rate to reach £500,000.

### Executive Answer

**Driver 2 - COGS stickiness and gross margin collapse - Second largest driver:**

### Why It Happened (Drivers)
The first and largest driver was a sharp revenue contraction of £258,788.23, or -28.6% month-on-month. Within revenue, Amazon Sales fell from £390,197.19 to £166,829.60, a fall of £223,367.59 which accounts for 86.3% of the total revenue decline. Inter company sales to BC Ltd fell from £39,224.55 to £1,881.93, a fall of £37,342.62, with smaller falls in Ebay sales, Sales, and SLA & Contract Income. Website Sales-GWL was broadly stable at £277,069.07 vs £272,780.09.

The second driver was gross margin collapse due to COGS failing to scale with revenue. COGS fell by only £33,513.98, or -5.4%, while revenue fell -28.6%. As a result COGS as a share of revenue rose from 69.0% to 91.5%, and gross profit fell by £225,274.25, or -80.4%. This £225,274 gross profit loss explains 94.2% of the total net profit decline. The connected accounting ledger records this cost stickiness, but specific operational, supplier, or pricing reasons for the elevated COGS are not recorded in the financial ledger.

The third driver was a £15,602.94 increase in operating expenses, up 30.0% month-on-month, which turned an already weak gross result into an operating loss. The largest increases were Staff wages up £6,767.26 from £18,454.42 to £25,221.68, Regulatory, Subscriptions & Licensing Fees up £5,216.62 from £2,117.77 to £7,334.39, and Insurance up £1,590.00 from £259.10 to £1,849.10, plus Employer NI up £1,190.33 and Locum & Contractor costs up £1,145.67. Gross margin moved -22.47 percentage points from 31.00% to 8.53%, and net margin moved -26.82 percentage points from 25.48% to -1.34%.

These are suggested actions, not facts.

Confidence is LOW for overall financial position and cash, as balance sheet and cash tools did not return data due to authentication failures. ## September Management Accounts – MI Health Ltd

### Executive Answer
September 2026 closed at a net loss of £7,975.32 on revenue of £645,516.57. The loss was driven by a thin gross margin combined with operating expenses exceeding gross profit. Source: Xero Live API, retrieved 2026-10-07.

### What the Data Shows
FACT from live Profit and Loss, period 2026-09-01 to 2026-09-30: Revenue was £645,516.57, all recorded under Sales Revenue. Cost of goods sold was £590,448.17. Gross profit was £55,068.40, a gross margin of 8.53 percent. Operating expenses were £66,926.43, comprised of Payroll Expenses of £42,000.00 and Rent and Utilities of £24,926.43. Operating profit was negative £11,858.03. Net profit was negative £7,975.32, a net margin of negative 1.24 percent.

FACT on year to date: The Profit and Loss for 2026-04-01 to 2026-09-30 returned identical totals to September alone. This indicates the connected ledger currently holds recordable trading activity for September only, with no additional amounts recorded for April to August in the live report response.

NO DATA, not zero, for financial position and cash: Live Balance Sheet, Bank Summary, Cash Flow Balance and Invoices endpoints returned authentication failures with status 401 AuthenticationUnsuccessful, and the cash flow summary returned DATA_NOT_AVAILABLE for operating, investing, financing and net cash change for April to September. I therefore cannot establish ending cash balance, net cash movement, receivables, payables, or working capital for September.

### Why It Happened – Drivers
The ledger proves what happened in profit terms. Gross profit of £55,068.40 was insufficient to cover operating expenses of £66,926.43, creating a shortfall of £11,858.03 at operating level before a £3,882.71 difference to net loss, with no other income recorded.

Within that, cost of goods absorbed 91.47 percent of revenue, leaving only 8.53 percent as gross margin. On expenses, Payroll accounted for 62.8 percent of operating expenses and 6.51 percent of revenue, while Rent and Utilities accounted for 37.2 percent of operating expenses and 3.86 percent of revenue.

The connected accounting ledger records the COGS and expense amounts but does not record specific operational, supplier or commercial reasons for the level of COGS or overheads, so the underlying business cause cannot be confirmed from ledger data alone.

### Supporting Calculations
CALCULATION: COGS ratio is £590,448.17 divided by £645,516.57 equals 91.47 percent. CALCULATION: Gross shortfall versus overheads is £66,926.43 minus £55,068.40 equals £11,858.03. CALCULATION: Payroll share of revenue is £42,000.00 divided by £645,516.57 equals 6.51 percent. CALCULATION: To break even on current overheads at current mix, required gross profit was £66,926.43 versus actual £55,068.40, a gap of £11,858.03, equivalent to approximately 1.84 pence per pound of revenue.

### CFO Interpretation and Recommendation
INTERPRETATION: September traded at scale on revenue but at a loss-making margin structure. With gross margin at 8.53 percent, overheads at 10.37 percent of revenue more than consumed trading profit. This is a margin leverage issue rather than a revenue volume issue for the month reported.

RECOMMENDATION as next steps, not as facts: Review COGS composition and pricing to test scope to lift gross margin by at least 1.9 points to cover the current overhead base. Review the £42,000 payroll base and £24,926 rent and utilities charge against capacity and contracts before committing to additional fixed cost. Re-authenticate the Xero Bank and Balance Sheet feeds so October management accounts can include cash, receivables, payables and reconciliation, since no cash assurance can be given for September.

### Data Confidence and Limitations
Confidence is HIGH for September Profit and Loss figures, which came directly from the live Xero ProfitAndLoss endpoint. Confidence is LOW for financial position, liquidity and cash movement, where live reports were unavailable due to API authorisation errors and DATA_NOT_AVAILABLE status. No accounting records were returned for balance sheet or bank balances, so I make no claim of zero cash or zero debt. All figures in GBP for MI Health Ltd, financial year ending March.

Gross profit of £55,068.40 was insufficient to cover operating expenses of £66,926.43, creating a shortfall of £11,858.03 at operating level. Payroll represented 62.8% of operating expenses and 6.5% of revenue, while Rent & Utilities represented 37.2% of operating expenses and 3.9% of revenue. ## Executive Answer

MI Health Ltd is loss-making across both September 2026 and October 2026 on live Xero data, with each period reporting revenue of £645,516.57 and a net loss of £7,975.32. The pattern is unchanged between the two months, with thin gross margin and operating expenses exceeding gross profit. Source: Xero Live API, retrieved 2026-10-07.

### What the Data Shows

For the period 01 September 2026 to 30 September 2026 and for the period 01 October 2026 to 31 October 2026, the Xero profit and loss report records identical results. Revenue is £645,516.57 from Sales Revenue, cost of goods sold is £590,448.17, gross profit is £55,068.40, operating expenses are £66,926.43, operating profit is negative £11,858.03 and net profit is negative £7,975.32. Operating expenses consist of Payroll Expenses of £42,000.00 and Rent and Utilities of £24,926.43. Other income is £0.00 in both periods.

Balance sheet and bank cash positions could not be established. Live Xero balance sheet and bank summary endpoints returned authentication failures, and the cash flow summary returned no usable monthly trends. I therefore cannot confirm ending cash, net cash movement, receivables, payables or equity, and I do not report cash as zero.

### Why It Happened

The loss is explained within the profit and loss ledger itself. Gross margin of 8.53 percent leaves £55,068.40 available to cover £66,926.43 of overheads, which creates an operating shortfall of £11,858.03 in each period. Payroll is the material overhead driver, followed by Rent and Utilities. The connected ledger records an improvement of £3,882.71 from operating loss to net loss, but with other income at £0.00 the specific tax, interest or adjustment reason is not recorded in the returned financial ledger.

### Supporting Calculations

Gross margin is 8.53 percent, calculated as £55,068.40 divided by £645,516.57. Operating expenses are 10.37 percent of revenue, calculated as £66,926.43 divided by £645,516.57, which exceeds gross margin by 1.84 percentage points. Net margin is negative 1.24 percent, calculated as negative £7,975.32 divided by £645,516.57. The October figures repeat September exactly to the penny, which for a period ending 31 October 2026 but retrieved on 07 October 2026 suggests incomplete month-end processing or draft data rather than two independent full months with identical trading.

### CFO Interpretation and Recommendation

The position points to structure rather than scale, since £645,517 of revenue still produces a loss in both periods. As suggested next steps, review pricing and purchasing because cost of goods absorbs 91.47 percent of revenue, review the £42,000 payroll base and £24,926 rent and utilities charge against activity levels, and re-authenticate the Xero bank connection so a full balance sheet and cash reconciliation can be completed. No recommendation is made on collections, cash or solvency because no authoritative balances were returned.

### Data Confidence and Limitations

Confidence is HIGH for revenue, cost of goods, gross profit, expenses and net loss, which come directly from the live Xero profit and loss reports. Confidence is LOW for overall financial position and liquidity because balance sheet and cash data were unavailable due to Live Xero API authentication errors. The October comparison should be treated as provisional until the month is closed in Xero.

### Executive Answer

Supplier payment lag across all fully paid bills averages 18.4 days from invoice date to fully paid date, with a median of 20 days.

### What the Data Shows

Source: Xero Live API, retrieved 2026-10-07.

FACT: 7 fully paid bills were analyzed covering 3 suppliers.

FACT: Overall average payment lag is 18.4 days, overall median is 20 days, with a range from -5 days to 36 days.

FACT by supplier:
AAH Pharmaceuticals Limited — 4 bills, average 20 days, median 24.5 days, range -5 to 36 days, total billed £44,500.
Acme Supplies Ltd — 2 bills, average 19.5 days, median 19.5 days, range 15 to 24 days, total billed £15,000.
Global Tech Services — 1 bill, average 10 days, median 10 days, total billed £2,500.

FACT at bill level:
AAH-102, AAH Pharmaceuticals, 2026-09-05 to 2026-09-25, 20 days, £18,500.
AAH-101, AAH Pharmaceuticals, 2026-08-01 to 2026-08-30, 29 days, £12,000.
AAH-103, AAH Pharmaceuticals, 2026-07-15 to 2026-07-10, -5 days, £5,000, recorded as temporal anomaly.
INV-1001, Acme Supplies, 2026-04-01 to 2026-04-16, 15 days, £5,000.
INV-1002, Acme Supplies, 2026-04-01 to 2026-04-25, 24 days, £10,000.
INV-1003, Global Tech Services, 2026-04-01 to 2026-04-11, 10 days, £2,500.
AAH-099, AAH Pharmaceuticals, 2026-01-10 to 2026-02-15, 36 days, £9,000.

### CFO Interpretation and Recommendation

Derived insight: AAH Pharmaceuticals shows the widest spread, with one bill at 36 days and one temporal anomaly where paid date precedes invoice date. Acme Supplies is consistent in the 15 to 24 day range. Global Tech Services is fastest at 10 days but based on a single bill.

Financial interpretation: The connected ledger records an average payment cycle under 3 weeks, which indicates payables are being cleared promptly. The -5 day record for AAH-103 is an unusual data pattern that requires audit review, as fully paid date should not precede invoice date, and may reflect a dating or allocation entry issue in Xero.

Recommended next steps are to review invoice AAH-103 for correct invoice and payment dates, and to confirm whether payment terms differ by supplier since AAH shows higher variability than the other two suppliers. The ledger does not record commercial reasons for timing differences.

### Data Confidence and Limitations

Confidence: HIGH that reported lags match live Xero invoice records for these 7 bills. Coverage is limited to fully paid bills with usable dates returned by the API, so unpaid or partially paid bills are not reflected in this timing analysis.

### Executive Answer
September 2026 management accounts are partial. Trading performance is confirmed from the live ledger, but financial position and cash cannot be confirmed because those Xero endpoints returned authentication failures.

Source: Xero Live API, period 01 September 2026 to 30 September 2026.

### What the Data Shows
Revenue for September was £645,516.57. Cost of sales was £590,448.17, leaving gross profit of £55,068.40. Operating expenses were £66,926.43, comprised of payroll of £42,000.00 and rent and utilities of £24,926.43. This produced an operating loss of £11,858.03 and a net loss of £7,975.32 for the month, with no other income recorded.

No accounting records were returned for balance sheet, bank balances, cash flow, or invoices and bills for September. The Live Xero API returned AuthenticationUnsuccessful for the BalanceSheet, BankSummary and Invoices resources, so I cannot establish actual values for cash, receivables, payables, inventory, or net assets. These are NO DATA, not confirmed zero.

### Why It Happened
What happened in September is that cost of sales absorbed 91.47 percent of revenue, leaving a gross margin of 8.53 percent that was insufficient to cover the operating expense ratio of 10.37 percent. The resulting shortfall explains the full operating loss.

Why cost levels were at those amounts cannot be determined from the ledger. The connected accounting ledger records the COGS and expense amounts, but specific operational, supplier, or commercial reasons are not recorded in the financial ledger.

### Supporting Calculations
Gross margin was £55,068.40 divided by £645,516.57, equal to 8.53 percent. Net margin was negative £7,975.32 divided by £645,516.57, equal to negative 1.24 percent. Payroll represented 62.76 percent of operating expenses, with rent and utilities representing the remaining 37.24 percent. The £3,882.71 difference between operating loss and net loss implies a non-operating benefit, the detail of which was not returned in the profit and loss payload.

### CFO Interpretation and Recommendation
The September structure lost 1.24p per £1 of sales because overhead exceeded available gross profit. This is a margin constraint rather than a revenue scale issue on the reported figures.

As suggested next steps, review COGS composition and pricing for September, hold discretionary overhead until gross margin recovers above the overhead ratio, and re-authenticate Xero for balance sheet and bank feeds so that a complete management pack with cash and working capital can be closed.

### Data Confidence and Limitations
Confidence is MEDIUM overall. Profit and loss facts are HIGH confidence as directly returned from Xero Live API. Financial position and liquidity are LOW confidence because required data was unavailable due to API authentication failure. No complete September management accounts can be certified until those feeds are restored.

## Executive Answer

A 20% fall in revenue on the current baseline would deepen the existing net loss from -£40,880.54 to -£45,570.72, an additional loss of £4,690.18. Source: Xero Live API.

### Actual Baseline

The baseline reflects actual performance for 1 April 2026 to 30 September 2026 retrieved from Xero at 2026-10-07T13:07:13.201Z. Actual revenue was £780,683.86 with actual COGS of £764,951.85, leaving actual gross profit of £15,732.01. Actual operating expenses were £58,156.33, resulting in an actual net loss of -£40,880.54. The business is therefore already loss-making at current revenue, with a very thin gross margin implied by COGS at approximately 97.98% of revenue.

### Assumption

The scenario assumes revenue decreases by 20% while COGS moves proportionally at a constant variable cost ratio of 97.98%. The formula applied is Scenario Revenue equals Actual Revenue multiplied by one minus 20%, and Scenario COGS equals Scenario Revenue multiplied by the variable cost ratio. Operating expenses are held fixed at £58,156.33, with no change in pricing mix, fixed cost absorption beyond Opex, tax, receivables collection, or cash effects modelled.

### Scenario Result

Under that assumption, scenario revenue is £624,547.09 and scenario COGS is £611,961.48. Scenario gross profit is £12,585.61 at a scenario gross margin of 2.02%. Scenario operating expenses remain £58,156.33. Scenario net profit is -£45,570.72. Scenario ending cash was not modelled and is not available in this run.

### Impact

Compared with actuals, gross profit declines by £3,146.40 and net profit declines by £4,690.18. In percentage terms this is a further 11.5% deterioration in net loss from an already negative base. The margin percentage is unchanged because the model holds the COGS ratio constant, so the entire gross profit reduction flows through to the bottom line against a fixed Opex base.

### CFO Interpretation and Limitation

This is a hypothetical what-if scenario model, not a forecast, budget, or guaranteed future outcome. The connected accounting ledger confirms what would arithmetically happen under the stated cost behaviour, but specific operational, supplier, or commercial reasons for any future revenue change are not recorded in the financial ledger. As a suggested next step, focus review on the sustainability of the current 2% gross margin and the coverage of the £58,156.33 Opex base, since any revenue contraction without COGS or Opex adjustment directly widens the loss.

### Data Confidence and Limitations

Confidence is HIGH for baseline and scenario arithmetic, with dataQuality reported as COMPLETE and calculation performed deterministically from Live Xero API data. Limitation is that ending cash and overdue receivables effects were not established in this scenario run, so no cash impact can be confirmed.

September 2026 was loss-making. The business generated £645,516.57 of revenue but reported a Net Loss of -£7,975.32, a Net Margin of -1.24%.

### What the Data Shows
Source: Xero Live API, period 2026-09-01 to 2026-09-30, retrieved 2026-10-07.

FACT: Revenue was £645,516.57, all recorded to Sales Revenue.
FACT: Cost of Goods Sold was £590,448.17.
FACT: Gross Profit was £55,068.40, Gross Margin 8.53%.
FACT: Operating Expenses were £66,926.43, comprised of Payroll Expenses £42,000.00 and Rent & Utilities £24,926.43.
FACT: Operating Profit was -£11,858.03.
FACT: Net Profit was -£7,975.32, Net Margin -1.24%.

### Why It Happened (Drivers)
The loss was driven by margin structure, not by revenue absence. Gross Profit of £55,068.40 was insufficient to cover Operating Expenses of £66,926.43, creating an operating shortfall of -£11,858.03.

Payroll Expenses at £42,000.00 represent 62.8% of Operating Expenses and 6.5% of revenue. Rent & Utilities at £24,926.43 represent 37.2% of Operating Expenses and 3.9% of revenue. COGS consumed 91.47% of revenue, leaving only 8.53% to contribute toward overheads.

### Supporting Calculations
COGS to Revenue: £590,448.17 / £645,516.57 = 91.47%.
Operating Expense to Revenue: £66,926.43 / £645,516.57 = 10.37%.
Gross Profit coverage of OpEx: £55,068.40 / £66,926.43 = 82.3%, leaving a gap of £11,858.03 at operating level.

### CFO Interpretation & Recommendation
The connected accounting ledger shows COGS increased to a level that leaves a thin gross margin, and operating expenses exceeded that margin. Specific operational, supplier, or commercial reasons for the COGS level are not recorded in the financial ledger.

Suggested next steps: review COGS composition and pricing to improve the 8.53% gross margin, and review the fixed overhead base of £66,926.43 against monthly gross profit run-rate. This is a recommendation, not a fact.

Payment lag from invoice date to fully paid date averages 18.4 days across all suppliers, with a median of 20 days, based on 7 fully paid bills retrieved live from Xero.

### What the Data Shows
Source: Xero Live API, retrieved at 2026-10-07T13:15:31.224Z. All 7 paid bills in Xero were analyzed across 3 suppliers.

AAH Pharmaceuticals Limited accounts for 4 bills totalling £44,500, with an average lag of 20 days and a median of 24.5 days, ranging from minus 5 days to 36 days. Acme Supplies Ltd accounts for 2 bills totalling £15,000, with an average lag of 19.5 days and a median of 19.5 days, ranging from 15 to 24 days. Global Tech Services accounts for 1 bill totalling £2,500, with a lag of 10 days.

At bill level, AAH-099 took 36 days from 10 Jan 2026 to 15 Feb 2026 for £9,000, AAH-101 took 29 days from 1 Aug 2026 to 30 Aug 2026 for £12,000, INV-1002 took 24 days from 1 Apr 2026 to 25 Apr 2026 for £10,000, AAH-102 took 20 days from 5 Sep 2026 to 25 Sep 2026 for £18,500, INV-1001 took 15 days from 1 Apr 2026 to 16 Apr 2026 for £5,000, INV-1003 took 10 days from 1 Apr 2026 to 11 Apr 2026 for £2,500, and AAH-103 shows minus 5 days from 15 Jul 2026 to 10 Jul 2026 for £5,000.

### Why It Happened
The overall average of 18.4 days is driven primarily by AAH Pharmaceuticals Limited, which represents over half of the bills by count and the majority of billed value. Within AAH, two bills at 29 and 36 days pull the average upward, while one bill at 20 days sits near the overall median and one bill records as a temporal anomaly. Acme Supplies Ltd is consistent in the mid-teens to mid-twenties range, and Global Tech Services is the fastest at 10 days on its single bill.

### Supporting Calculations
The difference between the overall mean of 18.4 days and median of 20 days indicates a fairly centred distribution with one negative outlier. AAH-103 is flagged as a temporal anomaly because the fully paid date precedes the invoice date, producing minus 5 days. Excluding that single anomaly would raise the AAH average and the overall average, so the reported averages should be read with that data quality point in mind.

### CFO Interpretation and Recommendation
From a working capital perspective, payment timing in the 10 to 36 day range suggests supplier settlement within roughly two to five weeks, with AAH showing the widest variability. As a suggested next step, review bill AAH-103 for date entry accuracy since the ledger records payment before invoice date but provides no operational reason for that sequence, and confirm whether settlement terms differ by supplier given that Global Tech Services cleared in 10 days while AAH extended to 29 and 36 days on two larger bills.

### Data Confidence and Limitations
Confidence is high that the lag figures reflect the connected accounting ledger, since all 7 paid bills were returned directly from the live Xero Invoices endpoint. The limitation is coverage, with only 7 bills and 3 suppliers, and the specific commercial or operational reasons for timing differences are not recorded in the financial ledger.
